children: , the biotechnology heavyweight behind Repatha and experimental olpasiran, inherited a tougher burden of proof as its shares stood at $437.23. Novartis's pelacarsen successfully lowered lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), but failed to cut major cardiovascular events in a Phase 3 trial, according to Reuters. That miss sends a blunt warning across the entire Lp(a) drug race: improving the laboratory number may not improve the patient outcome.

Amgen's OCEAN(a) outcomes study has finished enrolling 7,297 participants and is tracking coronary-heart-disease deaths, heart attacks and urgent coronary procedures over roughly five years. Olpasiran uses a different drug design and may target a different patient population, so pelacarsen's failure does not predict Amgen's result. It does, however, strip away any easy assumptions investors may have made about the commercial value of dramatic Lp(a) reductions.

The chart sharpens that risk: Amgen's $437.23 share price sits 19.54% above its GF Value estimate of $365.76, leaving less room for clinical disappointment. Amgen still has the financial muscle to keep pushing, backed by $10.1 billion in second-quarter revenue and $3.5 billion in free cash flow. But the market will no longer reward olpasiran for simply crushing a biomarkerthe drug must prove it can prevent the cardiovascular events that matter.

title: Amgen's 7,297-Patient Heart Bet Just Inherited a Higher Bar
